  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Amara was twenty-one years old and had been a surgical resident for just over a year, but the path that led her to the operating room had started four years earlier, during a hurricane that ripped through her coastal hometown. She had been seventeen, home alone when the storm surge trapped her on the second floor of her family’s house. For hours she listened to the wind tear at the roof, the water rising below her, the dark pressing in from every window. She had been certain she would drown. When the storm finally passed and the water receded, she found her neighborhood unrecognizable—houses collapsed, cars overturned, neighbors missing. She had survived, but something in her had broken that night, and she had never quite trusted the world to stay safe again.

Now, as a surgeon, Amara moved through a world of controlled chaos, but her own internal chaos had only grown. The first sign came during her intern year: a sudden, violent thunderstorm one afternoon while she was in the operating room. The sound of rain against the windows made her heart pound, her breath catch, and she had to grip the instrument in her hand to keep it steady. She had laughed it off then, told herself it was just the pressure of her first case. But it kept happening. Any weather that reminded her of the hurricane—heavy rain, humid stillness before a storm, the particular quality of light when a front moved in—sent her into a state of high alert. She began checking the forecast compulsively, and if rain was predicted she would arrive at the hospital hours early, afraid of being caught outside. Night shifts were the worst: the dark corridors of the hospital at 3 a.m. made her feel like she was back in that flooded house, and she often found herself hypervigilant, scanning the shadows for threats that weren’t there.

Her body had become a source of constant alarm. Ordinary sounds—a tray of instruments clattering, a door slamming down the hall—made her jump, and she had to consciously suppress the flinch. During surgeries, when a monitor beeped or a suction machine hummed unexpectedly, she felt her stomach drop and her hands tremble. She had started avoiding the hospital gym because the elevated heart rate from exercise felt too much like the panic that accompanied those physical reactions. Instead, she poured her energy into controlling what she could: her emotions. She kept her face neutral, her voice steady, even when inside she was terrified. She had become, her colleagues noted, exceptionally compliant—agreeing to every extra call shift, never pushing back when senior surgeons dismissed her ideas, because any confrontation felt like a threat to her precarious sense of safety.

The worst part was the story she told herself now. Amara had come to believe that the hurricane had not just frightened her—it had destroyed the person she was supposed to become. She felt hollowed out, incapable of trusting her own judgment. She would second-guess a suture choice, hesitate before making an incision, convinced that if she relied on herself she would make a catastrophic mistake. And beneath that, a deeper certainty: that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that no matter how carefully she planned, bad things would happen to her and to the people she cared for. She had tried to push through, to be the surgeon her training demanded, but the vigilance was exhausting. She had stopped seeing friends, stopped leaving her apartment except for work. Even there, she found herself scanning the faces of patients and families, searching for signs of disaster.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a moment of collapse in the hospital bathroom after a particularly loud thunderclap during a night shift. She had locked herself in a stall, hands shaking, and realized she could not keep pretending this was normal. She had heard about a clinic for trauma, but the idea of admitting she couldn’t rely on herself felt like another failure. Still, she made the call. She sat in the waiting room with her hands folded in her lap, trying to control the tremor in her fingers, afraid that the therapist would confirm what she already suspected: that her life was ruined, and she had no way to fix it. But part of her—a small, stubborn part that had survived the hurricane—hoped that maybe, just maybe, she could learn to trust herself again.
